prize_parts.citation: for theories of firm heterogeneity and selection that explain who exports, how resources are reallocated across firms, and how trade generates gains

statement.case_for: My preferred part is unchanged: a single-part B044 award to Helpman and Melitz. The achievement is both a discovery and an explanatory framework, which is the combination I value most. Melitz (2003) is an identifiable origin that put selection into exporting and reallocation across firms into a tractable general-equilibrium model. Helpman, with Melitz and Yeaple, extended it to the choice between exporting and foreign direct investment. The framework reorganised firm-level trade research, and its core qualitative predictions have been tested in many countries over more than twenty years. It also reaches into productivity, reallocation and growth, so its relevance is not limited to trade. The 2008 prize covered earlier increasing-returns trade theory, and this is a later and distinct advance. I am not using the five-member support for B044 as evidence of merit. I re-examined the attribution and maturity arguments and they still hold. After reading the round 1 files, my conclusion is that B044 has the cleanest credit boundary among the three serious candidates for which the maturity evidence is strong. I would word the citation around the theory of selection and gains from trade and not around the empirical exporter regularities, so it does not claim more than the two named laureates did.
statement.case_against: The credit boundary is contestable. Bernard, Jensen, Eaton and Kortum contributed closely related empirical and quantitative work that a two-name award leaves out, and Redding's quantitative extensions are also uncredited. Welfare magnitudes depend on functional-form assumptions such as Pareto productivity and CES demand, so the mechanism is better supported than the size of the gains. Krugman's 2008 prize may reduce some members' appetite for a second trade award, although I do not think it should count as duplication. The work is more theoretical than the quasi-experimental evidence behind B038, which is closer to my own empirical priors, so I have tried to avoid over-weighting familiarity in either direction. Finally, B044 has five explicit supporters, short of the six needed, and I do not treat that as a reason to change my view of the science.

responses.point: Fredriksson prefers B038 and treats the skill-premium, task and China-shock strands as one programme asking what determines labour-demand and who bears the adjustment. He names Hanson versus Dorn as the hardest call and says a trade-shock-only version is a fallback he would weigh.
responses.response: I take the one-programme reading seriously, and I agree the work has been important for credible empirical design and for policy. It is the candidate I would move to if B044 cannot be supported. My remaining hesitation is the three-name cap. A trio that keeps Katz to anchor the technology strand excludes Dorn from the China-shock papers, and a trio that includes Dorn drops the technology strand. Because the persistence of the trade-shock effects and the shift-share identification are still debated, I give B038 less weight on settled maturity than B044. That is a difference in weighting, not a claim that B038 is the weaker contribution. I would also say plainly that the evidence for it comes from design and replication, so a citation should state what the evidence established and not give a final verdict on magnitudes.

responses.point: Boppart prefers B038 with Autor, Hanson and Katz. He argues that Katz is needed so the technology strand is credited and that Dorn should displace Katz only if the committee deliberately splits the strands. He also sees B044 as building on Krugman's prize without duplicating it.
responses.response: I agree on Krugman, and I accept that Katz is the long-run anchor for the technology strand. Your conditional is the answer to the chair's question about what would make B038 my preferred part. If the committee decides the award is about the determinants of labour demand and can state a principled boundary for it, I would support Autor, Hanson and Katz. If it decides the award is the trade-shock evidence alone, I would support Autor, Dorn and Hanson. I could not support an unexplained compromise that credits neither strand cleanly. That question about the boundary is what separates my ordering from yours, not a disagreement about whether the empirical designs are credible.

responses.point: Hassler, as chair, prefers B037 with Kiyotaki and Moore as a two-author origin. He excludes Katz from B038 on overlap with the 2023 prize and keeps B044 as his first alternative because the credit gap around Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum cannot be resolved from the evidence.
responses.response: I agree that B037 has the cleanest attribution on the list, and I have moved it into my alternatives for that reason. I do not put it ahead of B044, because the support for the collateral-amplification channel is mainly through calibrated models and the debate about direct evidence is still open. B044's mechanism has more direct firm-level confirmation, and the exporter-selection predictions are well tested. On the Bernard et al. gap, I would define the award as the theory of selection and its general-equilibrium consequences, with Melitz as the clear origin and Helpman's exporting-versus-FDI work as the separable extension. That wording acknowledges the empirical contributions as foundational motivation without crediting them in the prize. I accept that this boundary is a judgement, as yours is for Gertler and Gilchrist. On Katz, I still read the 2023 prize as being about women's labour-market outcomes, so I treat the overlap with B038 as adjacency and not duplication.

responses.point: Strömberg prefers B037 and says that more weight on direct empirical confirmation would favour B038 over B037. His reservations about B044 are the credit shared with people outside the ballot and the dependence of welfare conclusions on functional-form choices.
responses.response: I share both reservations about B044 and have listed them against it. On the model-dependence point, I would separate the qualitative selection and reallocation mechanism, which is well confirmed, from the size of the welfare gains, which is not. The citation can be worded around the first and leave the second as an open quantitative question. I agree with your own test on B037: if direct evidence is the standard, B038 and B044 both do better than the collateral channel. I have therefore replaced B025 with B037 as my second alternative. B037's attribution is clean, whereas B025's credit is spread across at least eight names and members disagree on the third. I keep B037 behind B038 because the identification concern you accept is the thing that would weigh against it.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept a citation that names the theory of selection and gains from trade, with the empirical exporter facts and Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum recognised only as motivation, or will judge that boundary indefensible for a two-name award.
Whether Redding's quantitative contributions should be credited alongside Helpman and Melitz. I read them as later extensions, but I have not verified the priority boundary independently.
How much weight to put on the model-dependent welfare magnitudes relative to the confirmed qualitative mechanism.

Whether B038 can be given a principled boundary, either as a labour-demand award (Autor, Hanson, Katz) or as a trade-shock award (Autor, Dorn, Hanson), and how much the debated persistence of the China-shock effects should count against its maturity. If B044 cannot reach six votes I would accept one of those two B038 versions on the grounds stated above.

Whether adjacency to earlier prizes should count only when the earlier citation covered the same discovery. I think that is the right standard and it should apply equally to B044 (2008), B038 (2021, 2023, 2024) and B037 (2022). I rely on colleagues' descriptions of those citations and have not checked the scientific backgrounds myself.
statement.conflict_note: No documented connection to Helpman or Melitz, or to the credited names on B038 or B037, appears in my supplied profile. My frequent co-authors (Bayer, Anwar, Lindquist, Holmlund, Lochner, Bindler) are not credited on any shortlisted ballot. My field, labour economics and the economics of crime, is proximate to B038, and I disclose that as field proximity, not merit. I joined the committee in 2023, the year Goldin was recognised. That is not a tie to Katz or to any candidate, but it bears on the question of how the 2023 prize relates to B038. I treat all of this as disclosed and not adjudicated, and I see no need for recusal on any ballot.
